Synthetic Methods
Catalytic Asymmetric 1,4-Hydrocarbonation of 1,3-Enynes via
Photoredox/Cobalt/Chromium Triple Catalysis
Ju-Song Yang, Xing-Yu Wang, Yong-Yao Li, Fu-Min Zhang,* Xiao-Ming Zhang, and
Yong-Qiang Tu*
Abstract: A synergistic photoredox/cobalt/chromium
triple catalysis system for regioselective, enantioselec-
tive, and diastereoselective 1,4-hydrocarbonation of
readily available 1,3-enyne precursors was explored,
providing a modular synthetic platform for various
trisubstituted axially chiral allenes bearing an extra
central chirality. The protocol features a broad substrate
scope, good functional group tolerance, excellent selec-
tivity, and mild reaction conditions. Furthermore, a
possible reaction mechanism is proposed based on
numerous control experiments and density functional
theory calculations.
Introduction
Prochiral 1,3-enynes have received extensive attention in
various asymmetric synthetic transformations using 1,4-
difunctionalization procedures because of their multiple
reaction sites and easily availability.
[1–3]
In particular, the
catalytic asymmetric 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes has emerged as a method for accurately adding a
hydrogen atom and carbon or heteroatom moiety in sta-
tionary conjugate π systems.
[4–9,11]
Accordingly, various
transition metal (TM) catalysts (palladium,
[4]
rhodium,
[5]
copper,
[6]
scandium,
[7]
etc.) and organocatalysts
[9]
have been
developed to synthesize silyl-, boryl-, and aryl-substituted
axially chiral allenes via an ionic pathway (Scheme 1A, top).
However, in sharp contrast to these ionic pathways, the
radical 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes has yet to
be exploited owing to the canonical migratory insertion of
metal hydride into olefin units typically generating more
stable alkyl metal intermediates rather than dissociative
propargyl or short-lived allenic radicals.
[10]
To the best of
our knowledge, only one example has been reported; very
recently, Fu et al. achieved chiral nickel hydride–catalyzed
asymmetric coupling of prochiral 1,3-enynes with racemic
secondary alkyl electrophiles to simultaneously produce
central and axial chirality (Scheme 1B, bottom).
[11]
There-
fore, exploring new radical formation modes from 1,3-
enynes to achieve mechanistic innovations and obtain useful
multiple chiral allene architectures is urgent.
As the radical equivalent of Brønsted acid proton
transfer, TM-catalyzed (cobalt (Co), iron (Fe), manganese
(Mn), etc.) metal hydride hydrogen atom transfer (MHAT)
reactions of alkenes represent a powerful and practical
method for constructing diverse C � C and C-heteroatom
bonds.
[12–18]
Among them, tandem MHAT/1,2-addition was
developed by Shenvi et al. (2018)
[14]
and Shi et al. (2021)
[15]
to couple alkyl-substituted olefins, allenes, or 1,3-dienes
with radicalophilic imines or aldehydes, respectively. For the
catalytic asymmetric version, a recent breakthrough was
elegantly disclosed by Wang et al., employing modified
photoredox/Co/chromium (Cr) triple–catalytic systems for
enantioselective 1,2-addition of benzoyloxy-substituted 1,3-
dienes to synthesize aldehydes bearing an indispensable
benzoyloxy protecting group, in which the oxygen atom in
the substrates plays an essential coordination role
(Scheme 1B).
[16]
Retrospectively, MHAT-meditated regio-
and chemoselective 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of more
structurally complex 1,3-enyens substrates was rarely studied
except for a remarkable racemic version of research work by
Carreira’s group in 2006;
[17]
unfortunately, only azodicarbox-
ylate was used as an electrophile, which led to the
corresponding propargyl derivatives. To fill this gap, partic-
ularly the catalytic asymmetric version, we speculated that if
other electrophiles, such as aldehydes or imines, were
reacted with the chiral propargyl radical species derived
from prochiral 1,3-enynes, the unconventional asymmetric
1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes would occur; fur-
thermore, the novel synthetic method would provide an
efficient approach toward α-allenol, a unique structural
motif bearing both central and axial chirality, widely found
in natural products, pharmaceuticals, functional materials,
chiral ligands, and key synthetic intermediates (Fig-
ure 1).
[19–20]
However, this attractive strategy has several
synthetic challenges that must be addressed. 1) Unlike the
1,2-addition of an allyl group via a suitable six-membered
transition state, the 1,2-addition of propargyl-containing
intermediates to aldehydes via an extremely distorted cyclic
transition state leads to unmanageable regioselectivity,

Based on it, Glorius,

Wang

et al. have
elegantly realized alkylation and allylation of aldehydes via
reductive radical-to-polar cross-over process. Notably, the
more attractive redox-neutral three-component reaction of
terminal 1,3-enynes via a radical addition mode, was
successively established by Glorius and Wang et al., afford-
ing the racemic propargylated and chiral allenylated prod-
ucts, respectively (Scheme 1C).
[24d,27a]
Inspired by these and
MHAT chemistry, to develop a viable and alternative
manner to form essential propargyl radical, herein, we
report a protocol for radical-involved reductive coupling of
Z/E-mixed internal and terminal 1,3-enynes with aldehydes
via a tandem MHAT/1,2-addition transformation sequence
facilitated by a photoredox/Co/Cr triple–catalytic system
(Scheme 1D). This protocol successfully afforded opera-
tional connection between readily accessible 1,3-enyne feed-
stocks and multiple-substituted axially chiral allenes bearing
a C-stereogenic center, an important structural motif (Fig-
ure 1). Furthermore, mechanistic studies and density func-
tional theory (DFT) calculations revealed the origin of the
regioselectivity, diastereoselectivity, and enantioselectivity.
Results and Discussion
Optimization of Reaction C ondition
Based on our design, we commenced catalytic asymmetric
radical–involved reductive coupling studies using
triisopropyl(pent-3-en-1-yn-1-yl)silane (1 a) and benzalde-
hyde (2 a) as the model substrates. Initially, optimization
studies were performed using cobalt tetraphenylporphine
(CoTPP, 1 mol %), chromium(II) chloride (CrCl
2
,
13 mol %), and photosensitizer Ir-I (1 mol %) as the triple-
catalytic metal species, our developed SPD (L1) as a chiral
ligand, Hantzsch ester (HE) as the electron and proton
donor, and tetrahydrofuran (THF) (0.05 M) as the solvent.
The reactions were performed under 70 W blue light
emitting diode irradiation for 16 h. As expected, using L1 as
the chiral ligand resulted in the desired α-allenol 3 a in high
yield and good stereoselectivity (Table 1, entry 1), whereas
other nitrogen-containing ligands (L2–L9) were less effec-
tive (Table 1, entries 2–9). Subsequently, the reaction
solvents, MHAT catalyst, and other reaction parameters
were varied, respectively. Using dimethoxyethane as the
solvent caused a slight increase in yield (87 %) and stereo-
selectivity (96 % ee, and > 20 : 1 dr) (Table 1, entry 10),
whereas chlorinated solvents such as 1,2-dichloroethane and
chlorobenzene were unsuitable for this transformation
(Table 1, entries 11 and 12, respectively). Notably, minor
inseparable propargylation regioisomers were detected
when polar dimethylformamide was used as the solvent
(Table 1, entry 13). Furthermore, the reaction hardly pro-
ceeded using iron(tetraporphyrinato) chloride (FeTPPCl) or
tetraphenylporphyrinato Mn(III) chloride (MnTPPCl) as
the MHAT catalyst instead of CoTPP (Table 1, entries 14
and 15, respectively). The control experiments demonstrated
that all of the reagents and conditions in the synergistic
triple catalysis were required because no reaction occurred
when the light source, the photosensitizer, CoTPP, or CrCl
2
was separately removed (Table 1, entry 16). Therefore, the
reaction parameters listed in entry 10 (Table 1) were
selected as the optimal reaction conditions for further
investigations.
Investigation of the Substrate Scopes
Using the optimized reaction conditions, we first examined a
series of 1,3-enynes (Table 2). When the acetylenic substitu-
ents of the 1,3-enynes (triisopropylsilyl, tert-butyldimeth-
ylsilyl, and triethylsilyl groups) were varied, all reactions
proceeded smoothly to afford the corresponding silyl-
masked allenes 3 a–3 c, respectively, in good yields (87 %–
91 %) with excellent enantioselectivities (95 %–98 % ees).
Similarly, various 1,3-enynes bearing vinyl substituents,
including straight-chain amyl, cyclopentyl, phenyl, and
benzyl ether, were all successfully converted to the corre-

the expected product 5 p was obtained with excellent
selectivity, whereas ethyl 3-oxopropanoate led to the lactone
product 5 q via a tandem catalytic asymmetric MHAT/1,2-
addition/lactonization reaction sequence under similar reac-
tion conditions, providing a direct synthetic approach
toward chiral allenes bearing an adjacent chiral lactone unit.
Synthetic Application
To further confirm the robustness of this triple catalysis
system, late-stage diversification of structurally complex
molecules and commercially available chiral aldehydes was
performed (Figure 2A). Highly functionalized α-allenols 6 a–
6 c possessing continuous multiple stereogenic centers were
obtained as single diastereomers, predominantly determined
using enantioselective recognition of chiral SPD-series
ligands. Notably, the absolute configuration of product 6 b
was determined using X-ray single-crystal diffraction. More-
over, aldehydes derived from the anti-inflammatory drug
ibuprofen and the anti-inflammatory and antigout drug
probenecid were efficiently synthesized under optimal
reaction conditions, leading to products 6 d–6 f.

Mechanism Study
A series of control experiments were designed and con-
ducted to understand the triple catalysis system. First, in the
presence of radical scavengers (2.0 equiv. of allyl sulfone,
(2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidin-1-yl)oxyl (TEMPO), or 2,6-di-
tert-butyl-4-methylphenol (BHT)), the reactions were almost
entirely inhibited (Figure 3A). The 1,3-enynes 6 o containing
a three-membered ring, was subjected to the optimal
reaction condition, affording a ring-opening product 6 p in
~63 % yield. The possible formation pathway was as follows:
the 6 o initially occurred MHAT process to generate the
intermediate Int I, which fast collapsed toward intermediate
Int II. The radical Int II subsequently went through intra-
molecular 5-exo-dig cyclization to provide vinyl radical Int
III, which finally yielded the isolated product 6 p via H-atom
abstraction (Figure 3B). Moreover, cyclopropanecarbalde-
hyde smoothly produced the corresponding product 5 i
without the isolation of radical ring-opening coupling
product, except for the possibility of ketyl radical intermedi-
ates in the triple catalytic system. Subsequently, the results
of the interval light–dark reaction experiments and the
estimated quantum yield of Φ = 0.25, both indicated that the
current transformation occurred via a photoredox process
rather than a radical-chain pathway (Figure 3C). Therefore,
the propargyl radical species were unequivocally involved in
the current transformation. A linear correlation between the
enantioselectivities of α-allenol and the enantiopurities of

of the molecules (see Figure S7 for details).
[32b,d]
Overall, the
steric hindrance feature of the Cr–SPD–oxazoline catalyst
produces a stereoscopic pattern of 1,2-addition via a distinct
distorted cyclic transition state.
C onclusion
We developed a photoinduced Co/Cr dual-catalyzed 1,4-
hydrocarbonation reaction to couple prochiral 1,3-enynes
with radicalophilic aldehydes under mild, eco-friendly reac-
tion conditions, producing a series of axially chiral allenes
bearing a centrally chiral secondary alcohol unit in high
yields with excellent regioselectivity, enantioselectivity, and
diastereoselectivity. Mechanistic investigations and DFT
calculations were conducted to elucidate the origin of the
regioselectivity and stereoselectivity of this asymmetric
transformation.

Catalytic Asymmetric 1,4-Hydrocarbonation of 1,3-Enynes via

Ju-Song Yang, Xing-Yu Wang, Yong-Yao Li, Fu-Min Zhang,* Xiao-Ming Zhang, and
Yong-Qiang Tu*

Abstract: A synergistic photoredox/cobalt/chromium
triple catalysis system for regioselective, enantioselec-
tive, and diastereoselective 1,4-hydrocarbonation of
readily available 1,3-enyne precursors was explored,
providing a modular synthetic platform for various
trisubstituted axially chiral allenes bearing an extra
central chirality. The protocol features a broad substrate
scope, good functional group tolerance, excellent selec-
tivity, and mild reaction conditions. Furthermore, a
possible reaction mechanism is proposed based on
numerous control experiments and density functional
theory calculations.
Introduction

Prochiral 1,3-enynes have received extensive attention in
various asymmetric synthetic transformations using 1,4-
difunctionalization procedures because of their multiple
reaction sites and easily availability.<sup>[1–3]</sup> In particular, the
catalytic asymmetric 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-
enynes has emerged as a method for accurately adding a
hydrogen atom and carbon or heteroatom moiety in sta-
tionary conjugate π systems.<sup>[4–9,11]</sup> Accordingly, various

However, in sharp contrast to these ionic pathways, the
radical 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1,3-enynes has yet to
be exploited owing to the canonical migratory insertion of
metal hydride into olefin units typically generating more
stable alkyl metal intermediates rather than dissociative

propargyl or short-lived allenic radicals.<sup>[10]</sup> To the best of
our knowledge, only one example has been reported; very
recently, Fu et al. achieved chiral nickel hydride–catalyzed

secondary alkyl electrophiles to simultaneously produce

As the radical equivalent of Brønsted acid proton

elegantly disclosed by Wang et al., employing modified

enantioselective 1,2-addition of benzoyloxy-substituted 1,3-

benzoyloxy protecting group, in which the oxygen atom in
the substrates plays an essential coordination role
(Scheme 1B).<sup>[16]</sup> Retrospectively, MHAT-meditated regio-

Results and Discussion
Optimization of Reaction Condition

Based on our design, we commenced catalytic asymmetric
radical–involved reductive coupling studies using
triisopropyl(pent-3-en-1-yn-1-yl)silane (1 a) and benzalde-
hyde (2 a) as the model substrates. Initially, optimization
studies were performed using cobalt tetraphenylporphine
(CoTPP, 1 mol %), chromium(II) chloride (CrCl<sub>2</sub>,
13 mol %), and photosensitizer Ir-I (1 mol %) as the triple-
catalytic metal species, our developed SPD (L1) as a chiral
ligand, Hantzsch ester (HE) as the electron and proton
donor, and tetrahydrofuran (THF) (0.05 M) as the solvent.
The reactions were performed under 70 W blue light
emitting diode irradiation for 16 h. As expected, using L1 as
the chiral ligand resulted in the desired α-allenol 3a in high
yield and good stereoselectivity (Table 1, entry 1), whereas

tive (Table 1, entries 2–9). Subsequently, the reaction

solvent caused a slight increase in yield (87 %) and stereo-

chlorobenzene were unsuitable for this transformation
(Table 1, entries 11 and 12, respectively). Notably, minor

(Table 1, entry 13). Furthermore, the reaction hardly pro-
ceeded using iron(tetraporphyrinato) chloride (FeTPPCl) or
tetraphenylporphyrinato Mn(III) chloride (MnTPPCl) as
the MHAT catalyst instead of CoTPP (Table 1, entries 14
and 15, respectively). The control experiments demonstrated

Conclusion

We developed a photoinduced Co/Cr dual-catalyzed 1,4-
hydrocarbonation reaction to couple prochiral 1,3-enynes
with radicalophilic aldehydes under mild, eco-friendly reac-
tion conditions, producing a series of axially chiral allenes
bearing a centrally chiral secondary alcohol unit in high
yields with excellent regioselectivity, enantioselectivity, and
diastereoselectivity. Mechanistic investigations and DFT
calculations were conducted to elucidate the origin of the
regioselectivity and stereoselectivity of this asymmetric
transformation.
